content.text:
Today your outs depend on what went wrong.

| What happens | Your out today |
|---|---|
| A step fails | The panel shows the error with **Retry**, **Skip step** and **Skip case**. If the step itself is wrong, edit its block right there in the panel and press Retry. |
| The run seems stuck | It's waiting on you for one of four things: **Next** (step mode), a **✓ Pass / ✗ Fail** verdict, **Done** on a by-hand case, or **Allow / Deny**. Once the new runner reaches your tab, the status line says which. |
| You think the PR is broken | Press **✗ Fail**. That records the verdict with your note and moves to the next case. |
| You want out entirely | Press **Stop** twice. Verdicts so far are kept, and after a reload you get **Resume from case N**. |
| The graph or database is now in a weird state | No out from the page. You'd have to ask me in the terminal to re-run its setup, or run `db.ts reset`. |

**"Ask your agent"** opens a Claude window told which kit to drive. It can write steps for by-hand cases and fix a failed step. But it reaches the page only through Roam's Local API, which only the **Roam desktop app** has. In a browser tab it can't see or drive the page.

So the real gap is the last row. My recommendation is one out you never have to think about:

- **A "Stuck?" button**, always on the panel and the floating bar. It pauses the run and offers, in plain words:
  1. Try this step again (edit it first if it's wrong)
  2. Skip this step or this case
  3. "The PR is broken here": Fail with a note, then move on
  4. Hand it to Claude, with the case, the step, the error and the page state already in the prompt
  5. Start over clean
- **Start over clean** is the real reset: reload the tab, apply all of the kit's setup again (Roam-side and database), then Run. For the database part, the helper on this machine would run the kit's `publish`, `sql` and `rest` fixtures against the proof database, never shell commands. That makes every page run start from the same state, the way a terminal take does.
- **A kit-writing rule:** anything a case changes gets put back by setup at the start of every run, so a run that dies halfway can't leave things dirty. I'd fix ENG-2194's trigger and ENG-2267's node types to follow it.

That's a decent chunk of runner work, and it changes what the helper is allowed to do: a kit page could make it run SQL against the local proof database. Should I build it?

- design:accessibility-review: Run a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit on a design or page. Trigger with "audit accessibility", "check a11y", "is this accessible?", or when reviewing a design for color contrast, keyboard navigation, touch target size, or screen reader behavior before handoff.
- design:design-critique: Get structured design feedback on usability, hierarchy, and consistency. Trigger with "review this design", "critique this mockup", "what do you think of this screen?", or when sharing a Figma link or screenshot for feedback at any stage from exploration to final polish.
- design:design-handoff: Generate developer handoff specs from a design. Use when a design is ready for engineering and needs a spec sheet covering layout, design tokens, component props, interaction states, responsive breakpoints, edge cases, and animation details.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. # MANDATORY RULES — Check every session

## NEVER add Co-Authored-By
Never add `Co-Authored-By` lines to commits. All commits are sid's. No exceptions.

## NEVER cd out of the worktree
When the env says `Primary working directory: .../.claude/worktrees/<TICKET>`, all commands stay inside it. Bash cwd persists, and absolute `Edit` paths to `/mnt/data/projects/discourse-graph/apps/roam/...` silently target the MAIN repo on `main`. Use `git -C <worktree>` or `(cd ...; cmd)` subshells; never bare `cd` to the main repo path. See [[feedback_stay_in_worktree]].

## NEVER use git reset --hard
`git reset --hard` destroys untracked files that were accidentally staged in a prior commit.
Use `git restore` or `git checkout -- <file>` for targeted resets. If you absolutely must
reset, stash or back up untracked files first. NEVER run `git reset --hard` without asking.

## Ticket is the spec, code is the source of truth
The Linear ticket (description + comments) is the spec. The code is the source of truth for current behavior. Anything neither settles goes to sid as a question with a proposed default. Never read Roam design blocks, worklog pages, or other upstream traces to fill a gap unless sid names the UID in this conversation, even if a launcher or memory lists them as "read first". See [[feedback-ticket-is-spec-code-is-truth]].

## NEVER assume, ALWAYS look up
When the user references something by name ("accessors", "the helper", "that util", etc.):
1. **STOP. Do NOT assume you know what they mean from conversation context.**
2. **Search the codebase** (Grep/Glob) for the actual thing they're referencing.
3. Only proceed after you've read the actual code.

This applies especially when the user says "we already have X for that" — go find X before writing anything.

## ALWAYS run all three checks after changes
From `apps/roam/` (or worktree equivalent):
1. `npx eslint --max-warnings 0 <changed-files>`
2. `npx prettier --check <changed-files>`
3. `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck`

All three must pass. Don't skip `tsc` — example/test files reference exported types and will break on schema changes.

## PR workflow skills (2026-08-31, supersedes the michael-trio rule)
The old trio (/think-like-michael, /review-like-michael, /save-from-myself) is SUPERSEDED — /pre-pr-review covers them. Do not run the trio per PR anymore. Standing set:

**Per PR:**
1. `/pre-pr-review` — independent Opus pass, after push and after follow-up pushes (implementer self-review doesn't count)
2. `scope-check` — after review; produces the `## Scope check` section for the PR body (team template `.github/pull_request_template.md`)
3. `pr-video` — only if the PR is missing a demo for the template's Loom section

**During implementation:** `roam-global-tailwind` when styling Roam UI.
**Team-facing prose:** `dg-engineering-writing-style` always; tickets via `dg-create-engineering-ticket`.
**Never** use `ask-as-sid` on this project.
Curt directives ("minimal commit push") still skip the per-PR skills — see [[feedback_minimal_means_skip_skills]]. Details: [[feedback-pr-workflow-skills]].

## Follow findings to their conclusion
When reviewing code (especially during skill passes), if you observe facts that together imply a problem, STATE the problem. Don't list observations and move on.
- Trace return types through every call site. If a function always returns `T` (never undefined), then `?? fallback` is dead code at that site — even if other sites need it.
- "Unnecessary" = "remove it." Don't soften to "not harmful."
- "Consistent with other sites" is not a reason to keep dead code.

## Minimize reviewer cognitive load
- Don't rearrange existing code unnecessarily.
- Don't extract variables that are only used once.
- Keep diffs minimal: only change what's needed for the task.

Base directory for this skill: /mnt/data/projects/discourse-graph/.claude/skills/dg-engineering-writing-style

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.
